chapter_summary.text: This chapter introduces whole numbers up to the millions. It covers place value, reading and writing numbers in words and figures, rounding and estimation, multiplying and dividing by tens, hundreds and thousands, order of operations and solving word problems.

learning_objectives.text: Read and write whole numbers up to 9,999,999 in figures and words.
Identify the place value of any digit in a whole number.
Round numbers to the nearest 10, 100 or 1 000 and make reasonable estimates.
Multiply and divide whole numbers by 10, 100 or 1 000 using place‑value reasoning.
Apply the order of operations correctly.
Solve word problems involving addition, subtraction, multiplication and division of whole numbers.

meaning.text: The value of a digit depending on its position (units, tens, hundreds, etc.).
A single numeral (0‑9) that makes up a number.
Replacing a number by a nearby value that is easier to work with.
The rule that multiplication and division are done before addition and subtraction.

explanation.text: The book shows numbers broken into place‑value cards (hundred‑thousands, ten‑thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens, ones) and asks pupils to state the value of a digit in its position.

core_lessons.title: Writing Numbers in Words and Figures

explanation.text: Students convert numbers such as 124 936 into words ("one hundred twenty‑four thousand, nine hundred thirty‑six") and vice‑versa.
Numbers are rounded to the nearest 10, 100 or 1 000 by looking at the digit to the right of the rounding place. Estimates are then used for quick calculations.

core_lessons.title: Multiplying by Tens, Hundreds or Thousands

explanation.text: Multiplying a whole number by 10, 100 or 1 000 shifts each digit to the left, adding the appropriate number of zeros.

core_lessons.title: Dividing by Tens, Hundreds or Thousands

explanation.text: Dividing a whole number by 10, 100 or 1 000 shifts each digit to the right, removing the corresponding zeros.
The book stresses doing multiplication or division first (from left to right) and then addition or subtraction.
Real‑life scenarios are modelled with bar diagrams and solved using the operations learned.
Each digit moves one place to the left, adding a zero at the end.
Each digit moves two places to the left, adding two zeros.
Each digit moves three places to the left, adding three zeros.
First multiply by 7, then attach a zero (multiply by 10).
Break the divisor into 10 and 3, divide step by step.
The tens digit (6) is 5 or more, so round the hundreds up.
Round each factor to a convenient number and multiply.
First find the number of bags, then the sales amount, finally subtract the cost to get profit.

misconception.text: When a number is exactly halfway between two rounding targets, some pupils round down.

correction.text: If the digit to the right of the rounding place is 5 or more, always round up (e.g., 16 500 rounds to 17 000).

misconception.text: Multiplying by 100 adds two zeros to the original number regardless of its size.

correction.text: Multiplying by 100 shifts every digit two places left; zeros are added only if needed to keep the place values correct.

misconception.text: In the order of operations, addition is done before multiplication.

correction.text: Multiplication and division are performed first (left to right), then addition and subtraction.

answer.text: "four hundred thirty‑five thousand, six hundred seventy‑two"

question.text: What is the value of the digit 8 in 72,845?
Evaluate $9 + 3 \times 6$ using the order of operations.
A book costs $849. Round to the nearest hundred dollars.

review_checklist.text: I can read and write whole numbers up to millions in both figures and words.
I can state the value of any digit in a whole number.
I can round numbers to the nearest 10, 100 or 1 000 correctly.
I can multiply and divide whole numbers by 10, 100 or 1 000 using place‑value reasoning.
I can apply the order of operations to solve mixed‑operation problems.
I can solve word problems by modelling them with diagrams and the appropriate calculations.
